_about: Every idea this project has tested, one entry per study. Read by dashboard/server.py for the Research tab. Add an entry when a study finishes; numbers come from each study's write-up (the 'doc'). verdict: live = something from it is on a live test; failed; finding = a result worth keeping that isn't a trading rule.
lessons: Ideas work in the years their research was based on, then fade once published. That happened in stocks, currencies, bonds and countries.
Risk can be predicted, direction can't. The move-size model beat both simple guesses; no direction model did.
What held up is the stock market's own return, taken with more risk while the trend is up (leveraged trend). That's a risk choice, not skill.
Fancier math (hidden-state models, lasso, boosted trees, random-matrix cleaning) didn't beat simple rules.
Combining many weak signals, the way quant funds do, also failed in large stocks. The one input that keeps pointing the right way is the price of crash protection in options.

studies.name: S&P 500 move size
studies.idea: Predict how big tomorrow's S&P 500 move will be (a range, not a direction) from volatility, dealer gamma and the Fed, CPI and jobs calendar.
studies.result: Backtest of 3,151 days: about 4% smaller error than both simple guesses, and its 90% ranges caught 90.3%. Live since Nov 9.
studies.lesson: The one model here that clearly beats its baselines, because it predicts risk, not direction.

studies.name: Gamma breakout tracker
studies.idea: When a big stock breaks above its largest call strike and holds for 30 minutes on heavy volume, dealer hedging should push it further.
studies.result: Live since Nov 9. Predictions are rare (about one a week), so there are far too few to judge.
studies.lesson: At this pace a verdict needs more than six months.

studies.name: Political game machine
studies.idea: Simulate the 2028 primaries and general election, and compare the chances with betting markets.
studies.result: 509 forecasts logged. None settle until 2028.
studies.lesson: Candidate ratings are researched drafts the owner hasn't reviewed. Feedback is years away.

studies.name: Stock direction from options prices
studies.idea: Each week, the chance each S&P 500 stock beats SPY, from what options traders pay (calls vs puts, crash protection) and last week's move.
studies.result: No version reliably beats the base rate. The price of crash protection pointed the right way in all four looks, weakly. Three versions log live from Nov 17.
studies.lesson: Most published option signals are dead in large stocks. One weak survivor, not yet proven.

studies.name: Volatility-managed market
studies.idea: Hold more of the market after calm months and less after wild ones (Moreira & Muir 2017).
studies.result: 1937-2026: 9.3% a year against 10.7% for just holding. Worse in 4 other markets and 42 of 49 industries.
studies.lesson: It cuts crash losses but misses the rebounds. The paper's result rests on 1926-1936.

studies.name: Nine classic published strategies
studies.idea: Momentum, value, size, low volatility, industry momentum, trend and others, long-only, on 100 years of data.
studies.result: None beats the market after costs. The 10-month trend rule is safer, not better: since 2006, 9.7% a year against 11.3%, worst drop -18% against -50%.
studies.lesson: Edges shrank by a third to two-thirds after publication. The 10-month trend is on the live paper record.

studies.name: Risk budget: stocks and Treasuries by equal risk
studies.idea: Pick a risk level, weight stocks and 10-year Treasuries by equal risk, drop either in a downtrend.
studies.result: 1965-2026: lost to plain SPY plus T-bills at the same risk, at every risk level.
studies.lesson: Since 2011 Treasuries have earned almost nothing above T-bills.

studies.name: Pairs trading
studies.idea: Buy the laggard and short the leader among the 20 closest same-sector stock pairs, and wait for them to converge.
studies.result: 2017-2026: -0.5% a year beyond T-bills after costs. Only 42% of trades converged.
studies.lesson: A famous 1990s edge that's been traded away.

studies.name: Macro timing
studies.idea: Average the predictions of 14 economic indicators to decide how much stock to hold.
studies.result: Worked 1947-2005 (14.1% a year against 11.9%). Failed 2006-2025 (8.7% against 11.1%, and -67% in 2008).
studies.lesson: Economic indicators stopped timing the market once the research was known.

studies.name: Tournament of 24 strategies
studies.idea: Nine more rules (leveraged trend, dual momentum, option overlays and others), then all 24 on the same years against SPY.
studies.result: None beats SPY by the rules. Leveraged trend made the most money ($109k against $77k from $10k, 2006-2025) and passed its confirmation on fresh markets and the real SSO fund.
studies.lesson: Leveraged trend earns more by taking more risk while the trend is up. Its worst drop over 100 years was -56%. It's on the live paper record.

studies.name: Trend across many markets
studies.idea: The 10-month trend rule on stocks, foreign stocks, bonds, property and commodities, long-only and long/short.
studies.result: Long-only made 4.8% a year. Half SPY, half long/short matched SPY's Sharpe ratio overall and trailed it since 2013.
studies.lesson: A plain 60/40 mix had a better Sharpe ratio than either.

studies.name: Overnight-only investing
studies.idea: Hold SPY only from the close to the next open, since most of its gain came overnight.
studies.result: After a 0.01% cost per trade: 4.6% a year against 10.8%. Since 2009 it loses even with free trading.
studies.lesson: Two trades a day is enough to erase a real pattern.

studies.name: Earnings-week premium
studies.idea: Hold each S&P 500 stock only on the three days around its earnings report.
studies.result: No premium: -0.02% a day against the same stocks on other days. $10k became $5.2k after costs against SPY's $44.7k.
studies.lesson: A small run-up in the five days before reports exists, but it's smaller than trading costs.

studies.name: Fed-day drift and the Fed cycle
studies.idea: Stocks used to rise in the day before Fed decisions, and in even weeks of the Fed's meeting cycle.
studies.result: Close-to-close drift: +0.46% in 2002-2011, +0.10% since 2012. The cycle failed after 2017. The 2 pm-to-2 pm window still showed +0.20% a meeting in 2016-2026.
studies.lesson: Faded after publication. The 2 pm window is on the live paper record, to be judged after 30 meetings.

studies.name: Constant leverage
studies.idea: Always hold 2x the US market.
studies.result: 1927-2026: 12.4% a year against 10.2%, but -98.7% in 1929-32, so it fails the safety rules. Monthly savers at 2x came out ahead of 1x in all 60 forty-year periods.
studies.lesson: Leverage helps someone saving steadily far more than someone investing a lump sum. Adding the 200-day rule cut the worst drop to -56%.

studies.name: Math exploration
studies.idea: Eight advanced methods: market-stress measures, hidden-state models, the options fear premium, lasso, random-matrix portfolios, boosted trees.
studies.result: None cleared the luck test on 1946-2005. The fear premium passed weakly on 2006-2026 ($127k against $89k), then failed its confirmation in other markets and other declines.
studies.lesson: The fear premium's edge came from 2000-02 and 2008 alone.

studies.name: Currency strategies
studies.idea: Carry, dollar carry, fair value, Taylor rule, momentum and trend across 9 major and 13 emerging currencies.
studies.result: Strong before 2006 (dollar carry had a Sharpe ratio of 0.99). All six finalists failed on the unseen years: -1.4% to +0.4% a year for the majors.
studies.lesson: Currency premiums faded after 2008.

studies.name: Global government bonds
studies.idea: Carry, value, momentum, trend and yield-curve timing across 10 countries' 10-year bonds.
studies.result: Weak even in 1980-2005. The one finalist lost money in 2016-2026, including -12% in 2022.
studies.lesson: Bond premiums were thin to begin with.

studies.name: Country stock-market rotation
studies.idea: Rotate among 22 country funds by momentum, value, low volatility or trend.
studies.result: Trend across countries made 4.4% a year in 2011-2026 against SPY's 14.0%. Country momentum lost 2.9% a year.
studies.lesson: It looked great in 1997-2010, which was US stocks' lost decade.

studies.name: Polymarket long-shot bias
studies.idea: Long shots are said to be overpriced in betting markets. Sell them (or buy heavy favourites) and hold to the end.
studies.result: 1,076 markets over three weeks. Long shots came in slightly less often than priced (1.3% against 2.6%), within luck. After the bid-ask cost both rules made about +0.4% a bet, no different from zero.
studies.lesson: Short-lived Polymarket prices were close to fair. Could be rerun in six months on markets first seen after Nov 16.

studies.name: The signal stack: 27 weak signals combined
studies.idea: What quant funds do: combine many weak published signals (momentum, reversal, low risk, trading activity, calendar, earnings, options) on S&P 500 stocks, each pointed the way its paper says, with equal weights.
studies.result: 2017-2026: the top fifth of stocks made 9.7% to 10.5% a year against SPY's 15.0% and 12.1% for every stock in equal amounts. The long-short version lost about 5% a year.
studies.lesson: Signals favouring smaller, less-traded stocks were badly wrong while the giants led. Crash protection pointed the right way for the fifth time. Company-accounts signals weren't tested.
